3. Content creation

Content creation capability helps Queensland Government employees create, edit, improve and manage digital content responsibly. It supports effective communication, service delivery, knowledge sharing, innovation and problem-solving through the purposeful use of digital technologies.

Official DigComp 3.0 area description

To create and edit digital content. To improve and integrate information and content into an existing body of knowledge while understanding how copyright and licences are to be applied, adopting an ethical and responsible approach in the creation, improvement and integration of digital content. To know how to apply computational thinking and programming techniques to give instructions to a computer system.

Why this area matters

Queensland Government employees create digital content every day, including briefs, reports, procedures, presentations, web content, records, dashboards, forms, guidance material, data products and communication resources.

Strong capability in this area helps employees create clear, accessible, accurate and responsible content. It also supports better information sharing, improved service delivery and more effective use of digital tools, including approved AI-enabled tools.

Using workplace tools

Tool availability and approval varies across agencies.

Employees should only use approved content creation, collaboration, automation and AI-enabled tools in accordance with agency requirements, information security, privacy, copyright, accessibility and recordkeeping obligations.

3.1 Developing digital content

What it is

Creating and editing digital content in different formats. This includes developing documents, presentations, spreadsheets, forms, images, videos and other digital resources, as well as improving and adapting existing content for different audiences and purposes.

In practical terms, this means being able to answer:

"How can I create digital content that is useful, clear and fit for purpose?"

rather than simply:

"How do I make this document?"

Why it matters in Queensland Government

Queensland Government employees create digital content every day to inform decisions, deliver services, communicate with stakeholders and support business operations.

Good digital content helps:

  • Communicate information clearly
  • Improve decision-making
  • Support collaboration and knowledge sharing
  • Reduce confusion and rework
  • Improve customer and stakeholder experiences
  • Increase accessibility and inclusion
  • Improve productivity and efficiency

Digital content no longer consists solely of documents. Public servants increasingly create and maintain dashboards, online forms, presentations, collaboration spaces, visualisations, videos and AI-assisted content.

Strong content development skills help ensure information remains accurate, accessible, useful and appropriate for the intended audience.

Workplace scenarios

You may be demonstrating this competency when you:

  • Create a briefing package that combines written advice, visual information and supporting evidence for executive decision-making.
  • Produce accessible digital content that meets government standards and can be used by diverse audiences.
  • Develop content with assistance from approved AI tools while reviewing and refining outputs for accuracy and relevance.
Tools and processes

Tool availability and configuration differ between agencies. Use only systems approved by your agency.

Common tools

Tools are the digital technologies used to create, edit and publish content.

Examples include:

  • Microsoft Word
  • Microsoft PowerPoint
  • Microsoft Excel
  • Microsoft Forms
  • Microsoft OneNote
  • SharePoint
  • Power BI
  • Microsoft Copilot
  • Image, video and design tools approved by your agency
  • Web content management systems

Common processes

Processes are the ways of working that help ensure content remains accurate, useful and fit for purpose.

Examples include:

  • Planning content before creation
  • Identifying audience requirements
  • Applying accessibility principles
  • Using approved templates and branding
  • Reviewing and editing content
  • Incorporating feedback
  • Maintaining version control
  • Applying plain language principles
  • Testing content before publication
  • Updating content when information changes
Apply this competency at work
  1. Select an existing document, presentation, form or other piece of content you recently created.
  2. Review it from the perspective of its intended audience.
  3. Identify whether the content is clear, accurate and easy to understand.
  4. Check whether headings, formatting and structure support readability.
  5. Consider whether the content is accessible and inclusive.
  6. Identify one improvement that would make the content more useful.
  7. Implement the improvement.
  8. Ask a colleague for feedback on the revised version.

Hint: Good content development is not about creating more content. It is about creating content that helps people understand, decide, act or learn.

DigComp 3.0-aligned proficiency guide

DigComp 3.0 describes eight proficiency levels grouped into four broad bands. For simplicity, this Hub presents the four bands: Basic, Intermediate, Advanced and Highly advanced. The descriptions below are practical workplace interpretations of DigComp 3.0 and are not verbatim reproductions of the official competence statements.

Basic

With guidance as needed, individuals can:

  • Create simple digital content using common tools.
  • Edit or update existing digital content.
  • Understand that different types of content serve different purposes.
  • Recognise basic principles of accessible and effective content creation.

Intermediate

Individuals can:

  • Create digital content in a variety of formats.
  • Adapt content for different audiences and contexts.
  • Combine information from multiple sources to develop content.
  • Use digital tools confidently to create and edit content.
  • Improve existing content to make it more useful and effective.

Advanced

Individuals can:

  • Develop high-quality content for complex needs and audiences.
  • Select the most appropriate format for different communication purposes.
  • Support others in developing digital content.
  • Apply accessibility, usability and design principles.
  • Improve content creation processes and outcomes.

Highly advanced

Individuals can:

  • Design and lead complex digital content initiatives.
  • Develop new approaches to creating and managing content.
  • Guide others in advanced content development practices.
  • Evaluate and improve organisational approaches to content creation.
  • Support innovation in digital content development.
Test your capability

Content Improvement Challenge

Choose a document, presentation, form, SharePoint page or report that you regularly use.

Using the downloadable template:

  • Identify the audience and purpose.
  • Assess the structure and readability.
  • Review accessibility and usability.
  • Identify opportunities to improve clarity.
  • Revise the content.
  • Seek feedback from at least one colleague.
  • Record lessons learned.
  • Identify one content-development skill to improve further.

3.2 Integrating and re-elaborating digital content

What it is

Modifying, refining, combining and building upon existing digital content to create new content, knowledge or solutions. This includes integrating information from multiple sources, adapting content for different audiences and purposes, and adding value through improvement, analysis or creative reuse.

In practical terms, this means being able to answer:

"How can I use existing content to create something better, more useful or more relevant?"

rather than simply:

"How can I copy and paste this information?"

Why it matters in Queensland Government

Queensland Government employees rarely start with a blank page.

Most work involves bringing together information, data, documents, policies, stakeholder input, research and lessons learned from multiple sources to create new outputs and insights.

Strong content integration skills help employees:

  • Reduce duplication of effort
  • Reuse existing knowledge effectively
  • Create better quality work products
  • Improve consistency across the organisation
  • Save time and resources
  • Produce evidence-based advice and recommendations
  • Translate information for different audiences
  • Generate new insights from existing information

As AI-powered tools become increasingly common, employees also need the ability to critically review, modify and improve content generated by digital technologies rather than simply accepting it as-is.

Workplace scenarios

You may be demonstrating this competency when you:

  • Combine information from multiple reports into a single resource tailored for a specific audience.
  • Transform complex data into visual summaries that support decision-making and stakeholder understanding.
  • Update existing guidance material to reflect policy changes while retaining important historical context.
Tools and processes

Tool availability and configuration differ between agencies. Use only systems approved by your agency.

Common tools

Tools are the digital technologies used to combine, modify and improve content.

Examples include:

  • Microsoft Word
  • Microsoft PowerPoint
  • Microsoft Excel
  • Microsoft Copilot
  • SharePoint
  • OneNote
  • Power BI
  • Microsoft Loop
  • Forms and survey platforms
  • Approved design and content creation tools

Common processes

Processes are the ways of working that help ensure integrated content remains accurate, useful and appropriate.

Examples include:

  • Reviewing existing content before creating new content
  • Identifying authoritative sources
  • Synthesising information from multiple sources
  • Adapting content for different audiences
  • Updating and improving existing resources
  • Seeking feedback and incorporating improvements
  • Validating AI-generated outputs
  • Maintaining references and source information
  • Checking consistency across documents and resources
  • Applying accessibility and usability principles
Apply this competency at work
  1. Select a current work activity that requires information from multiple sources.
  2. Identify at least three existing resources relevant to the task.
  3. Review the information for accuracy, relevance and currency.
  4. Identify common themes, key messages or insights.
  5. Create a short summary, briefing, presentation or visualisation that combines the information.
  6. Adapt the content for your intended audience.
  7. Ask a colleague to review the final output.
  8. Identify how the integrated content provides greater value than the individual sources.

Hint: Integrating content is not about combining everything you can find. It is about selecting, refining and connecting information so that it becomes more useful to the audience.

DigComp 3.0-aligned proficiency guide

DigComp 3.0 describes eight proficiency levels grouped into four broad bands. For simplicity, this Hub presents the four bands: Basic, Intermediate, Advanced and Highly advanced. The descriptions below are practical workplace interpretations of DigComp 3.0 and are not verbatim reproductions of the official competence statements.

Basic

With guidance as needed, individuals can:

  • Make simple modifications to existing digital content.
  • Combine information from a small number of sources.
  • Use templates or existing resources to create new content.
  • Recognise that content can be adapted for different purposes.

Intermediate

Individuals can:

  • Modify, refine and integrate content from multiple sources.
  • Adapt digital content for different audiences and contexts.
  • Create new content by building on existing information and resources.
  • Combine data, information and content to support work activities.
  • Improve content created by others, including AI-generated content.

Advanced

Individuals can:

  • Create new knowledge and insights from diverse sources of information.
  • Adapt and repurpose content for complex situations and audiences.
  • Evaluate and improve integrated content for accuracy, quality and usability.
  • Support others to combine and improve digital content effectively.
  • Use digital technologies to create value from existing information and resources.

Highly advanced

Individuals can:

  • Design new approaches for integrating and improving digital content.
  • Lead activities that combine content, data and knowledge across multiple sources.
  • Support innovation through creative reuse and adaptation of digital content.
  • Guide others in advanced content integration practices.
  • Contribute to improvements in organisational knowledge management and content reuse.
Test your capability

Content Transformation Challenge

Choose a current document, report, dataset or collection of resources relevant to your work.

Using the downloadable template:

  2. Assess the strengths and limitations of each source.
  3. Identify key themes or messages.
  4. Create a new output tailored to a different audience or purpose.

  6. Review the content for clarity, relevance and accessibility.

3.3 Copyright and licences

What it is

Understanding how copyright, licences and related legal and ethical requirements apply to digital content. This includes knowing when content can be used, shared, adapted or published, recognising different licence conditions, attributing sources appropriately and respecting the rights of content creators.

In practical terms, this means being able to answer:

"Am I allowed to use, adapt, share or publish this content?"

rather than simply:

"Can I access or copy this content?"

Why it matters in Queensland Government

Queensland Government employees regularly create, adapt, share and publish digital content.

This may include:

  • Reports
  • Presentations
  • Images
  • Graphics
  • Templates
  • Videos
  • Data
  • Website content
  • Training materials
  • AI-assisted or AI-generated content

Not all digital content can be freely copied, changed or distributed. Copyright applies automatically to many types of original content, and licence conditions determine what others can do with that content. Australian copyright guidance explains that copyright protects original expression in forms such as writing, images, music, films and software code, and gives copyright owners exclusive rights such as copying, publishing and communicating the material.

Strong copyright and licence awareness helps employees:

  • Use digital content lawfully and ethically
  • Reduce legal and reputational risk
  • Respect creators' rights and moral rights
  • Attribute sources appropriately
  • Understand when permission may be required
  • Use Creative Commons and open government material correctly
  • Avoid inappropriate reuse of third-party material
  • Make better decisions when using AI-generated content

Queensland Government generally supports the distribution and reuse of government material, but some content is excluded from Creative Commons licensing, including logos, trademarks, third-party material and material with other specified licence conditions.

Workplace scenarios

You may be demonstrating this competency when you:

  • Confirm that images, datasets or documents can be reused before including them in a published government resource.
  • Apply correct attribution requirements when incorporating third-party content into presentations or reports.
  • Advise a project team on copyright considerations when using AI-generated or externally sourced material.
Tools and processes

Tool availability and configuration differ between agencies. Use only systems approved by your agency.

Common tools

Tools are the digital systems, platforms or resources used to create, reuse, licence, attribute or publish content.

Examples include:

  • Microsoft Word, PowerPoint and Excel
  • SharePoint and intranet publishing platforms
  • Website content management systems
  • Microsoft 365 stock images, icons and templates
  • Creative Commons licence information
  • Queensland Government website copyright statements
  • Australian Government and Queensland Government open data portals
  • Approved AI tools
  • Agency-approved image, design or media libraries
  • Referencing and citation tools

Common processes

Processes are the checks and decisions that help ensure content is used lawfully, ethically and appropriately.

Examples include:

  • Checking copyright and licence statements before reuse
  • Confirming whether content is government-owned, third-party or open licensed
  • Attributing sources when required
  • Checking whether Creative Commons conditions allow the intended use
  • Seeking permission where no licence or exception applies
  • Reviewing whether content can be adapted, edited or redistributed
  • Labelling AI-generated content where appropriate
  • Keeping records of source material, permissions and licence conditions
  • Checking whether logos, branding or trademarks are excluded from reuse
  • Applying agency approval processes before publishing or distributing content
Apply this competency at work
  1. Choose a piece of digital content you want to reuse, such as an image, graphic, table, template, report extract or dataset.
  2. Identify where the content came from.
  3. Check whether the source includes a copyright or licence statement.
  4. Determine whether the content is Queensland Government material, Australian Government material, third-party material, open licensed content or AI-generated content.
  5. Check whether the licence allows your intended use, including copying, adapting, sharing or publishing.
  6. Identify whether attribution is required.
  7. Check whether any exclusions apply, such as logos, branding, trademarks, images or third-party material.
  8. Decide whether you can use the content, need to attribute it, need permission or should choose a different source.

Hint: If content is publicly available online, that does not automatically mean it is free to reuse. Always check the copyright and licence conditions before copying, adapting or publishing content.

DigComp 3.0-aligned proficiency guide

DigComp 3.0 describes eight proficiency levels grouped into four broad bands. For simplicity, this Hub presents the four bands: Basic, Intermediate, Advanced and Highly advanced. The descriptions below are practical workplace interpretations of DigComp 3.0 and are not verbatim reproductions of the official competence statements.

Basic

With guidance as needed, individuals can:

  • Recognise general copyright and licence concepts in digital contexts.
  • Recognise that original digital content is automatically protected by copyright.
  • Identify that different types of copyright and licences may apply to digital content, including AI-generated content.
  • Recognise that AI-generated content should be labelled as such where appropriate.
  • Use and share digital content while following basic legal and ethical guidelines.

Intermediate

Individuals can:

  • Recognise that copyright and licensing in digital environments can be complex and should be approached carefully.
  • Distinguish between copyright, trademarks, patents, designs and other intellectual property concepts at a general level.
  • Check licence terms before using, adapting or sharing digital content.
  • Apply Creative Commons or similar open licence conditions correctly.
  • Attribute sources and creators appropriately.
  • Identify when permission may be required before reuse, adaptation or publication.

Advanced

Individuals can:

  • Evaluate copyright and licence conditions across different types of digital content.
  • Apply legal, ethical and organisational requirements when reusing or adapting content.
  • Make informed decisions about using third-party, government, open licensed or AI-generated content.
  • Support others to understand and apply copyright and licence requirements.
  • Identify risks associated with inappropriate reuse, attribution or publication of digital content.

Highly advanced

Individuals can:

  • Develop or improve approaches for managing copyright and licensing in digital content workflows.
  • Guide teams in applying copyright, licence and attribution requirements consistently.
  • Support responsible use of open licences, Creative Commons and government-owned content.
  • Lead improvements in how digital content is sourced, attributed, reused and published.
  • Contribute to organisational practices that support lawful, ethical and transparent content reuse.
Test your capability

Copyright and Licence Check

Choose a digital resource you are planning to use in a work product.

Using the downloadable template:

  1. Record the content title, source and URL or location.
  2. Identify the content type, such as image, document, data, video, template or AI-generated content.
  3. Check the copyright or licence statement.
  4. Identify what the licence allows.
  5. Identify any restrictions, exclusions or attribution requirements.
  6. Decide whether the content can be used as-is, adapted, shared or published.
  7. Record the attribution statement you would use.
  8. Identify whether permission, review or an alternative source is required.

Download: Copyright and Licence Check Template (Excel)

  • Australian Government Attorney-General's Department - Copyright basics

  • Australian Government Attorney-General's Department - For copyright users

  • Microsoft Support - What am I allowed to use premium creative content for?
    Explains how Microsoft 365 premium images, icons and creative content can be used within Microsoft 365 files and SharePoint, and highlights limits on using that content outside Microsoft 365 contexts.
  • QUT Copyright Guide - Introduction
    Provides a plain-language overview of copyright, moral rights, Creative Commons licences and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property considerations. Useful for building broader copyright awareness before reusing digital content.
  • DigComp 3.0 - Copyright and licences 3.3
    Provides DigComp-aligned competence statements and learning outcomes for copyright and licences, including copyright, licensing, AI-generated content and ethical reuse of digital content.
Reflection questions

After completing this competency section, consider:

  • Do you usually check copyright or licence conditions before reusing digital content?
  • How do you decide whether content can be copied, adapted or shared?
  • What types of content do you reuse most often in your work?
  • What licence conditions or exclusions are most relevant to your role?
  • How confident are you in writing a correct attribution statement?
  • How should AI-generated content be labelled or reviewed before reuse?
  • What is one improvement you could make to your copyright and licensing practices?
  • Which DigComp proficiency statement best reflects your current capability?

3.4 Programming

What it is

Planning, creating, modifying or understanding sequences of instructions that digital systems can follow to solve a problem or perform a task. This includes computational thinking, automation, low-code tools, formulas, scripts and simple workflows.

In practical terms, this means being able to answer:

"Can I describe the steps a digital system needs to follow to solve this problem?"

rather than simply:

"Can I write code?"

Why it matters in Queensland Government

Programming is not only for software developers. For many public servants, this competency is about understanding how digital tools, automation, formulas and workflows can improve everyday work.

Queensland Government employees may use programming-related thinking when they:

  • Break a process into logical steps
  • Use formulas in Excel
  • Create a Power Automate flow
  • Build a simple Power App
  • Set up rules, conditions or branching logic
  • Use AI tools to help draft, test or explain logic
  • Work with technical teams to describe business requirements
  • Identify opportunities to automate low-value manual work

Strong programming and computational thinking skills help employees:

  • Improve inefficient processes
  • Reduce repetitive manual tasks
  • Communicate more clearly with technical teams
  • Understand how digital systems make decisions
  • Test whether a digital workflow produces the expected result
  • Build confidence with low-code and automation tools
  • Identify where automation is useful and where human judgement is still required

Queensland Government's Digital Service Standard includes expectations relevant to building or significantly altering digital information, products and services, including understanding user needs, tools and systems, security, accessibility, open standards, testing and performance improvement.

Workplace scenarios

You may be demonstrating this competency when you:

  • Map a manual administrative process and identify steps that could be automated safely and efficiently.
  • Break down a complex business problem into smaller components to design a digital solution.
  • Create or refine a simple workflow, automation or script to improve consistency and reduce manual effort.
Tools and processes

Tool availability and configuration differ between agencies. Use only systems approved by your agency.

Common tools

Tools are the digital technologies used to create, test or run instructions, workflows, formulas, automations or low-code solutions.

Examples include:

  • Microsoft Excel formulas and functions
  • Microsoft Forms branching logic
  • Power Automate
  • Power Apps
  • Power BI calculations and transformations
  • SharePoint lists
  • Microsoft Planner and workflow integrations
  • Approved AI tools
  • Agency-approved scripting, automation or development tools
  • Business process mapping tools

Common processes

Processes are the ways of working that help ensure digital instructions, formulas, automations and workflows are useful, reliable and safe.

Examples include:

  • Breaking a problem into smaller steps
  • Mapping inputs, actions, decisions and outputs
  • Writing clear business rules
  • Testing formulas, flows or workflows before use
  • Checking results against expected outcomes
  • Documenting how an automation works
  • Reviewing errors and making improvements
  • Considering security, privacy and access requirements
  • Escalating complex or high-risk automation to technical specialists
  • Monitoring whether a digital solution continues to work as intended
Apply this competency at work
  1. Choose one small repetitive work task.
  2. Write down the task as a sequence of steps.
  3. Identify the input, such as an email, form response, file, date or spreadsheet value.
  4. Identify the action, such as saving a file, sending a notification, updating a list or calculating a result.
  5. Identify any decision points, such as "if approved", "if overdue" or "if the value is above a threshold".
  6. Identify the output you expect.
  7. Test the steps manually using one example.
  8. Consider whether the task could be improved using a formula, template, flow, form or other approved digital tool.
  9. Record one risk or limitation that should be considered before automating it.

Hint: Programming starts with clear thinking. If you can describe the steps, decisions and expected outcomes clearly, you are already applying programming concepts.

DigComp 3.0-aligned proficiency guide

DigComp 3.0 describes eight proficiency levels grouped into four broad bands. For simplicity, this Hub presents the four bands: Basic, Intermediate, Advanced and Highly advanced. The descriptions below are practical workplace interpretations of DigComp 3.0 and are not verbatim reproductions of the official competence statements.

Basic

With guidance as needed, individuals can:

  • Recognise that digital systems follow instructions.
  • Identify simple steps needed to complete a task.
  • Understand that instructions must be clear and ordered.
  • Use simple formulas, rules or automated functions in familiar tools.

Intermediate

Individuals can:

  • Break a task or problem into logical steps.
  • Create or modify simple digital instructions, formulas, workflows or automations.
  • Use low-code or no-code tools to support routine work.
  • Test whether instructions produce the expected result.
  • Identify and fix simple errors in formulas, workflows or logic.

Advanced

Individuals can:

  • Design more complex workflows, formulas or automations to meet a business need.
  • Use conditions, variables, rules or structured logic to improve a digital process.
  • Test and refine digital instructions across different scenarios.
  • Support others to understand or use simple automation and programming concepts.
  • Identify when technical or specialist support is required.

Highly advanced

Individuals can:

  • Design or improve complex digital solutions using programming, automation or low-code approaches.
  • Lead or contribute to initiatives that improve digital processes through automation or structured logic.
  • Guide others in applying programming and computational thinking concepts.
  • Evaluate risks, limitations and impacts of automated or programmed solutions.
  • Contribute to organisational improvements in digital process design and automation.
Test your capability

Process-to-Automation Challenge

Choose a small, low-risk work process that is repetitive or rule-based.

Using the downloadable template:

  1. Describe the current process.
  2. Identify the trigger that starts the process.
  3. Map each step in order.
  4. Identify any decision points.
  5. Identify the expected output.
  6. Identify what could be automated using an approved tool.
  7. Test the logic using an example.
  8. Record risks, limitations and approval requirements.
  9. Decide whether the process should remain manual, be simplified or be explored for automation.

Download: Process-to-Automation Planner (Excel)

Reflection questions

After completing this competency section, consider:

  • What routine tasks in your work follow clear steps or rules?
  • Can you describe the task as inputs, steps, decisions and outputs?
  • Which parts of the process require human judgement?
  • Which parts could potentially be supported by a formula, flow, app or automation?
  • What risks would need to be considered before automating the process?
  • How confident are you in testing whether a digital workflow works as expected?
  • What is one small automation or logic skill you could practise next?
